utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can hear you and understand you and I'm also very sorry about what happened on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate your apologising. Yes, appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager, good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Morning, Your Honours I'm John Ackerman and I'm here with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Any preliminaries before we bring in the witness and finish with him? No? We go in -- I think we need to bring down the curtains for a while, until he comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The usher is going to give you the text of the solemn declaration which you are kindly requested to repeat before you recommence your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With regard to your contention that you saw Mr. Brdjanin at Manjaca, was there ever a time that any investigator or lawyer from the Office of the Prosecutor showed you a page of photographs to see if you could identify the person who you claim to have been Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Was such a possibility even mentioned or suggested to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did any Prosecutor or investigator show you a photograph of Mr. Brdjanin at any time prior to your testimony here on Friday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That visit to Manjaca by the person who you claim to be Brdjanin, who I put to you was Kupresanin, you said happened closer to the end of your stay there than the beginning, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it was not long after that visit that Manjaca was closed and you were freed, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the same thing happened at Omarska, didn't it? Not very long after the visit of the delegation that you described, where you heard about the delegation being there and heard the noise and stuff outside, very short time after that, Omarska was closed and you were transferred to Manjaca, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not really recall the time when that happened in Omarska, whether it was towards the end or sometime in the course of it. I just can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you were at Manjaca and the winter time came, you were given winter jackets by the ICRC, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The International Red Cross issued us with training suits, with foot wear, but there were no winter jackets. No, I think it seems to me that we did get those jackets but it was the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And that -- the day that you were -- that you left Manjaca, it was in December and it was cold and you were wearing those jackets, weren't you, all of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We saw a videotape, little segment of a video of a wedding here on Friday. And during the Prosecutor's questioning of you it was indicated that those little excerpts were prepared by you. Could you tell us how you prepared those? How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took only those parts of that videotape about which I'm -- which I knew that had gone missing. I mean they simply -- no. About those people that I knew were missing. I mean those are people whose trace was lost sometime in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That part I understood. I'm asking you more of a technical question, technically how was it done? Were you working with a video technician somewhere? Was that here at the Tribunal? How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here. It was here. I did it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you did it in conjunction with somebody, a technician who knew how to do that sort of thing or did you know how to do it yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a technician, somebody who knows how to do that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any questions? Thank you. That brings to us an end of your -- except that there is a couple of questions from Judge Taya.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: When did you come to know the fact that Mr. Brdjanin was arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about Mr. Brdjanin's arrest in 2001, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Through what way you knew about that fact? Through media, through someone? Through what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through media. I -- I could hear Radio Free Europe in the place that I live in, on the news.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Before you became to know the fact that Mr. Brdjanin was arrested, did you have anticipated that Mr. Brdjanin would be arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, can I ask you to repeat your answer? Because it was not picked up by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT27 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I assumed that Mr. Brdjanin might be arrested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That brings us to the end of your testimony here, after which you can return to your country. I'm sorry that we had to keep you for the weekend here. At the same time it was necessary. I also ought to inform you that at the beginning of this sitting, before you entered the hall, Mr. Brdjanin said that he was sorry for what happened last time. You will now be escorted by the usher, but before you leave this courtroom it is my duty as the Presiding Judge to thank you for having accepted to come and give evidence in this trial. Thank you. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stay where you are for the time being. Stay, stay, stay. You have one curtain which did not come down. The next witness is in closed session, if I remember well?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we get to Mr. Sejmenovic, as a result of the length of his testimony, last time --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- the only matters that I'm going to go through, I'm going to summarise again his evidence as I've done with other witnesses. There has been an objection to part of the testimony he gave which related to Mr. Brdjanin. One of those objections arises from the assembly of the 12th of May, so I'm going to go through that document in full. Your Honour, I should add and I add this now so that everybody is clear, Mr. Sejmenovic has -- this will be the fifth time he has testified. One of the reasons I'm not going to go through other documents that I could use with him is that I've taken the view that it would be unfair to keep him here talking about these events again for as long as it otherwise would take. He was cross-examined at length in the Stakic case, which is also contained in the transcript. So, Your Honour, on this occasion, I'm going to ask that Your Honours say that cross-examination is limited so that it doesn't cover the same ground that has already been covered. Clearly, it's most desire that Mr. Sejmenovic finish his evidence by Wednesday in any event because there will be no further sitting for a week. Your Honour, the other matter before he's called is this: Many of the Stakic exhibits are already exhibit numbers in this case. So in order -- what we've done, and we've provided to Mr. Ackerman I think we better provide it to Your Honours' legal officers, is a cross-reference because when one of the difficulties of not having the witness go through the exhibits again is it may be difficult to realise that there has actually been evidence about exhibits in this case. I know that Your Honours will have read through all the transcripts, but it may not have been obvious that nearly every single exhibit mentioned in the Stakic case is also exhibited in our case and already has exhibit numbers. So, Your Honour, with that introduction, the witness can be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before I comment on part of your statement, Mr. Ackerman, may I -- do you want to say anything about your -- the way you will conduct your cross-examination or whether you would agree with Ms. Korner to limit it to what has not already been stated upon cross-examination? I know that you are not the counsel cross-examining the witness in Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it may be that Mr. Sejmenovic has testified here five times before and that it's a burden on him to come testify but we didn't call him. The Prosecutor did. The agreement that we had regarding the use of transcripts from other cases was that they would serve as direct examination and I would be entitled to a full cross-examination. No one has ever cross-examined him before on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin and that's what I intend to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's bring Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree. I'm not saying for one moment that in matters strictly relating to Mr. Brdjanin, of course, but what I will be objecting to and I make it absolutely clear is that if we go over again the TO in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if the Prosecutor is abandoning the joint criminal enterprise theory, then I'll restrict it to Brdjanin only. If they are staying with it then I must do a complete cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And once more, welcome to this Tribunal, with which you are by now familiar. As I would imagine you are familiar with the very beginning of this procedure, that is the making of -- the entering of a solemn declaration. The solemn declaration is contained, the text of the solemn declaration is contained in the piece of paper that you've just been given by the usher and could you kindly read that statement aloud. And that will be your undertaking with this Trial Chamber to speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Since you have given evidence in more than one case already, I don't need to explain to you what the procedure is, and I would invite Ms. Korner now to start with her direct. Ms. Korner, I know that the practice that you have been adopting, not just you, but each one of you, is to go through parts of the transcript upon which you then intend putting questions. You can restrict that part to the events, proper events, on which you are then going to ask questions. I think it will cut shorter. The other thing that I think you ought to know, both of you, is that at least as far as I'm concerned, I am familiar with the transcript from Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is Your Honour telling me that you've read the nine days worth of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have gone through that transcript. That much. But I am not familiar with the contents of the statements of witnesses in other proceedings. In other words, if you will be making reference to any of those other statements, other testimonies, please let me know, a little bit in advance, so that I can bring them over and have a look at them because I haven't seen those.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. As I said originally, we are going to put in only the transcript on which we rely and in this case, we took the view that the Stakic transcript covered just about every aspect of Mr. Sejmenovic' life. Your Honour, the reason I'm doing that is because I'm well aware of the difficulties of following evidence through a transcript. Equally, the witnesses can't suddenly be thrown into cross-examination without some chance just to remind himself, and therefore, I don't think it takes very long and I think it's better that at least we summarise the major parts of the evidence that he's going to give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Try to keep it -- condense it as much as you can so that we try and finish with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no doubt at all this witness will be finished by Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good. Good to hear that, Ms. Korner. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have very serious doubt that he will be finished by Wednesday. I will also be offering as exhibits the transcripts from all the other cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in their entirety or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to be referring to parts of them but I think in their entirety they ought to be admitted properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At least if you're going to be referring to parts and you know which parts, if you can indicate those to us, we can be better prepared by the time you come to -- to your cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can probably do that although not immediately. Maybe during the break I can prepare it or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We will be happy if you could do that by tomorrow, by tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, let's see how we get along and, I think, rather than discuss how long this is going to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, good morning. I think your full name is Mevludin Sejmenovic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you born on the 15th of October of 1962?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think that you are a Bosniak by nationality?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, just so that the Court fully understands, Mr. Sejmenovic, I think that you have testified first of all in the Tadic case?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then in the case against Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were brought back for cross-examination in the -- what's called the Keraterm case?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sikirica and others. And you testified in full in the Stakic case a few months ago?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to summarise your background. I think it's correct that you were in 1990 -- I'm sorry, perhaps we ought to go back, yes. No. In 1990, were you elected as the first vice-president of the SDA in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At that stage, were you living in the Trnopolje area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can I have a translation?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. It was my fault. I hadn't put the thing on. Were you in the 1990 elections elected as the member for Prijedor to the republic assembly in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you attend that assembly as well as the Prijedor Municipal Assembly until the events of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All the sessions of the republic parliament and most sessions of the municipal parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And before the Serbs, the Bosnian Serbs, left the republic assembly in October of 1991, did you get to know the politicians in that assembly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did meet some of them. I met some of them personally. I knew others by sight. Or I got to know them by listening to their participations in the debate in parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, let's move straight away, please, to the accused in this case, Radoslav Brdjanin. When did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I first met him in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you first came across him, did you speak to him? Did you have any conversations with him?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I do not recall that we personally ever conducted any kind of conversation. Perhaps this did happen but I don't recall anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, in his speeches or discussions within the assembly, what were the sort of views he was putting forward?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, as one of the more prominent Members of Parliament, is a person I noticed only in the second half of 1991, when the debate took place on federal institutions, on the Yugoslav People's Army, and particularly the need to regionalise Bosnia-Herzegovina. As far as I can remember, that's when Mr. Brdjanin spoke more often in the debate. As for the proposals to start reorganising the country or rather establishing regions, he was one of the most prominent speakers and as a matter of fact he insisted the most that such proposals be put through parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just expand a little on what you mean by regionalisation?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: In that period of time, that is to say at the moment when the SDS MPs, primarily through Mr. Brdjanin, presented their demand that parliament approve the regionalisation of the country, in that stage, the SDS called that economic regionalisation. And they explained the need to do so due to economic necessity. There were many debates in parliament and it was pointed out that there was already regionalisation based on the economic principle. Other parties agreed that this be discussed by having this model perhaps corrected. However, the SDS wanted a completely different model of regionalisation. They presented some of their own parameters, but it all boiled down to the following: That they wanted to create regions along the lines of the already-established Serb regions in Croatia. Of course it was noticed that they started doing this in some parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina even before this had been discussed in parliament. So in Herzegovina they had already established a Serb region, the SAO Herzegovina and they had already taken some measures with a view to creating the same kind of region in the area of Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: From the point of view of your party or you in particular, what did the purpose of this regionalisation appear to be, if not economic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose was national, ethnic, and this was evident in the policy of the SDS of Croatia, in the area of the neighbouring country where there were Serb areas. They first called for economic regionalisation and then they closed off that area and turned it into Serb Autonomous Regions. So we already had experience with the SDS policies in the wider area and we also had experience in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you say that Brdjanin was one of the proponents of this regionalisation. What sort of position did he appear to hold within the SDS, in the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Until the debate on regionalisation took place, to be quite frank, I considered Brdjanin to be a very ordinary MP in parliament without any special kind of influence or any special kind of importance. Perhaps he did have that but I was not aware of it and I could not get such an impression because he was not particularly active, at least not at the outset, not at the first stage of parliamentary debates. However, when the debates on regionalisation started, then he was one of the most active speakers and that's when I concluded -- oh, yes and of course he was talking about very serious matters that could have very serious consequences. I came to the conclusion then that he probably had a stronger role in the SDS; perhaps he himself was struggling for that. But at any rate, he came to the forefront, or for example, he was one of the leading Members of Parliament among the SDS MPs. At least as far as parliamentary activities were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, one of the regions that was created, as we know about, was the Autonomous Region of Krajina with a seat, as it were, in Banja Luka. Did you become aware of Brdjanin within -- Brdjanin's position within that Autonomous Region?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: At first I didn't know that, only later when things were evolving further I found out that this region was formally established and this was disclosed in Banja Luka, and it became obvious that in this hierarchy in the Autonomous Region, Mr. Brdjanin also had a place. Of course Mr. Vojislav Kupresanin held the top position at the time. That the whole thing was organised and that it was going on before the parliamentary debate is something that I heard personally from Mr. Kupresanin. A few other MPs were present during the break, everybody was having coffee. On that occasion, Kupresanin was boasting to some of the other MPs of the SDS that he had done a lot and that Vucurevic had done something too in Herzegovina. And that other Serb MPs had not done anything except for talking. That's when Kupresanin said "We have already taken over the TV transmitter. We have already sealed off our own TV area. We are watching TV Belgrade. We have organised this." That is part of the conversation that I heard, and which clearly led me to the conclusion that this process was already well underway as far as this Serb region was concerned. Or rather this Autonomous Region as they formally called it later.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever during this period and up until May of 1992, see Brdjanin make speeches on television?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: During that period, I think that this did happen several times on the TV news because regionalisation was the main topic in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time and all the media and all the people who discussed this or rather --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour, to what he thinks happened several times. If he's just guessing, then it's not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you guessing? Or on what basis are you making your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the TV news were the most -- were the -- TV programmes in Bosnia-Herzegovina that were watched by most people at the time, and there were excerpts from parliamentary debates and there were interviews from -- with persons, important persons from various parties. Mr. Brdjanin certainly appeared there too as a member of parliament for Banja Luka that had just started setting up a region.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you actually see him yourself on television?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I think I saw him personally but I cannot recall which TV news, on which date. It would be very hard to remember exactly now. As a matter of fact, I think that I spoke in parliament and that I actually replied to Mr. Brdjanin and that we directly had a clash with regard to the issue of regionalisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did Mr. Brdjanin ever speak about the percentage of --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this, it's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have the question first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why is it leading?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He's asking if he spoke about percentage or something. If he heard him speak about something, he can say he did, but not to be led by Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Rephrase your question in a way in which it is not as leading as Mr. Ackerman imagines it is going to be, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to know what's leading about what I started to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. But any way, put the question and then if it's really leading, I will stop you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did Mr. -- did you ever hear Mr. Brdjanin speak about the proportion of the various nationalities that should be allowed to live in the area of the Bosnian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My objection is that that's excessively leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I await Your Honour's ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In parliament, during the first debates on regionalisation, Mr. Brdjanin mentioned many parameters supporting that theory. According to which the regions should be established. He spoke about the percentage of the population in Banja Luka, that it was a predominantly Serb area, about some economic parameters, about some percentages of economic resources that were going from Banja Luka to Sarajevo, leaving the Serb people in Banja Luka on the losing end. And therefore, in parliament, during this debate, he appeared to be the proponent of Serb interests exclusively in the area of Bosanska Krajina. That's what it looked like. As for other people, later on, when I was in Banja Luka, I heard from other people that on local TV, on radio and in the Banja Luka newspapers, Mr. Brdjanin appeared often, explaining that this was a Serb area which, over the past 40 or 50 years, through anti-Serb policies was populated by Muslims and that therefore the Serbs why imperilled and that they had to win their own national safety and security there and secure for themselves their own ethnic area. Since Mr. Brdjanin had a very symbolical type of speech, or rather he used adjectives often, he made statements that made the ordinary people very restless and very fearful. Often, these statements sounded like threats. I didn't hear it, but I heard from several people that Mr. Brdjanin said over the radio that the Muslims should not make sauerkraut that season because they won't need it that winter or that the Muslims should not buy firewood because they wouldn't need it that winter. At the same time, a campaign was organised to expel, move out, the non-Serb population from that area. At that time, in the Banja Luka media, people could read all the time about some kind of ratios, percentages, in terms of property on that territory, and that is something that happened in all towns where the Serbs took measures, not only in Banja Luka. The same thing happened in Prijedor. The same thing happened in Sarajevo. The same thing happened there where they said what was Serb and what percentage of the property there belonged to others and what percentage belonged to Serbs. And where non-Serbs lived in Serb ethnic areas, so non-Serbs were living there but they should leave and go to the place where they naturally belonged. Your Honours, it is very hard for me now so much time after that, to give you exact quotations. In a particular context, I may recall some but I'm interpreting the essence of what was being said, and sometimes I'm actually giving you the authentic statements that I heard at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Sejmenovic. I want to come back to Brdjanin as head of the Crisis Staff in a moment, but I want to just deal briefly with the evidence that you gave about the background to these events. I think you dealt with the referendum that took place in November or the plebiscite - I can never remember which is which - at page 4488 of the transcript in Stakic, you dealt with various documents and you dealt with your knowledge of Dr. Stakic at page 4526, and then why Prijedor was strategically important. Now, I want to move, please, to an assembly that took place in Banja Luka after Prijedor had been taken over on the 12th of May, and I'd like to you have P50, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he dealt with part of this in Stakic but part has been edited out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Since an objection was taken. Page 4623. Now -- Would Your Honours give me just one minute?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I know you weren't present, Mr. Sejmenovic, but I want to ask you about some of the personalities who spoke and some of the things that were said. And I think you've had a chance to have a look at it. Could you turn first of all to the speech made by Karadzic which you'll find on page 8? Firstly, have you heard Mr. Karadzic speak? I'm sorry, you won't find that on page 8. It's on the translation, page 8. It's -- it begins, "Ladies and gentlemen, deputies, honourable guests."

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I found that part.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now firstly, had you heard Karadzic speak in the assembly before the Serbs left?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I heard him speak before the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina the last time. I heard that he had spoken at the assembly that the Serb deputies held when they left the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina and this was on the TV news. In public --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I just want to know, because I want to ask you a general question. So you had heard him speak in the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, I want you to look at just part of what he said here. He said, "That the political conditions in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the last two years since the foundation of the HDZ, first in Croatia and then in Herzegovina and later in Bosnia too with its militant and dangerous gatherings with insignia of the Ustasha regime which has committed genocide against us and the setting up of the SDA at its founding assembly with a militant Islamic fundamentalism, et cetera." Had you heard him use language like that before?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Before, in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he did not use such wording.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had you heard him use such wording outside the parliament?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Outside the parliament, yes, in interviews, with some foreign journalists or domestic journalists, one could hear him use some of these terms, and one could read it in his statements carried by the written press. However, as time went by, this kind of vocabulary began to predominate in all Mr. Karadzic's public appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move, then, please, to the page 14 where he set out the strategic goals? Sorry it's page 14 in the English. And it's the paragraph that begins, "The Serbian side in Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do Your Honours have copies of the actual document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have it, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, but that's okay, Your Honour, I can follow it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was clearly on the list, I just neglected to bring it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But the important thing is I know that you can follow. All right. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you found that part?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In this, Karadzic part of the speech, Karadzic set out the six strategic goals, so called, or priorities. The first such goal is separation from the other two national communities, separation of states. Now, had you heard him utter those sentiments before?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No. Well, perhaps there were some hints, perhaps generally, but never directly and never as explicitly as this. Because at that stage, he usually spoke about the preservation of Yugoslavia rather than separation from other nations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then I don't think we need go through -- well, perhaps we can just summarise. The second strategic goal, the corridor between Semberija and Krajina. And then the third strategic goal, the corridor in the Drina valley. Fourth, the establishment of the border on the Una and Neretva Rivers, division -- fifth strategic goal, division of Sarajevo. And the sixth, the exit of the Serbian Republic to the sea. Then, if you go, please, to the paragraph that begins, "Honourable deputies, dear guests." This is page 21 of the English -- page 15 of the English. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: This is Karadzic again?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It says here -- just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of the difficulties is I was working off a different version when I was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It's halfway down -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, this is what I mean. It's halfway down the paragraph, that first paragraph. All right. Don't worry, the point I want it make out of this is not worth wasting time over. All right, could we go, then, please, next to the speech made by Mr. Milosevic, not, I hasten to add, I think the Milosevic, who is on trial. Do you know who that was, that Mr. Milosevic? Mr. Sejmenovic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I know there was some Milosevic. He was either in the cabinet in the government or in the parliament. I mean, the name sounds familiar or perhaps I just came across it in the press, but I believe he was one of the SDS officials -- I believe there was a MP called that, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. He, it would appear, was talking about the goal of setting up the corridor in Northern Bosnia, and if you go to the end of his speech, can you see the part that says, "I demand once again from the assembly to state its position on this strategic goal. And my proposal is the same as the one, no matter how megalomaniac it may be, which I presented to and which was accepted by the Presidency. Mr. Brdjanin is here, who was presiding in this Presidency. Mr. Radic was present. The Presidency has accepted that at the moment the right bank of the Sava River is our border with Croatia. Thank you, gentlemen, and I want the assembly to state its position on this." Had you heard discussion before of the right bank of the Sava River being the border with Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No. Not formally from SDS officials, but one could hear such utterances from members of the Serb Radical Party, who embraced the theory that wherever there were Serbs living, it was Serb territory and that in this war they should be Serbia or wherever there were some ancient Serb graves that would also be historic Serb turf and which should be liberated and joined with Serbia. As for the SDS, until that time, I did not hear it said in public. None of their officials, that is, ever said anything like that in public at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move, then, please, to somebody called Dragan Kalinic? This is at page 22 of the translation. Now, first of all, did you know Mr. Kalinic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, look at his speech and then I'll ask you about him or part of his speech. He said that amongst all the issues, this assembly should decide on, the most important is this: "Have we chosen the option of war or the option of negotiation? I say this with a reason and I must instantly add that knowing who our enemies are, how perfidious they are, how they cannot be trusted until they are physically, militarily destroyed and crushed, which of course implies eliminating and liquidating their key people. I do not hesitate in selecting the first option, the option of war." Et cetera. Now, had you heard Mr. Kalinic express sentiments like that before?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Until that time, Kalinic expressed views which were completely opposite. He was a prominent member of an opposition party, that is the Socialist Party or some other party, the SDP, yes, and he spoke in the parliament on behalf of the left wing. He used to be antiwar, anti-nationalist parties. And he very frequently spoke from that position. One could never hear anything like this from Mr. Kalinic when he spoke in the parliament, and I can tell you that when the Serb MPs walked out of the parliament and when we heard Mr. Kalinic was one of the few who left at the same time from the opposition, that is, and the public was shocked by his statements, that is, first by the fact that he had gone to Pale with SPS MPs and the SDS MPs and the members of the Serb Radical Party and also that he was rated very highly in that group and also the statements which he occasionally made for the media but shortly afterwards, he was elected as a minister, and I know that his party colleagues - I have some friends amongst them - simply could not believe that something like that could happen to Mr. Kalinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then later on, he stated, he gave his reasoning, for saying he wanted war. "They should go for war, the fate of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina cannot be solved in any other way but by war. It is possible that in doing this the fate of us Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina would be to choose 100 years of solitude over 500 years of slavery under some new Turkish empire." And finally he stated, "Why do I say that the option of war seems more likely to me? Because only what has been conquered militarily can become really and truly ours." And then I think we can skip the rest although he made various threats in relation to destruction of TV transmitters and the like. Now, can we turn, please, next in this to Mr. Vjestica? Miroslav Vjestica? Have you found that, Mr. Sejmenovic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: He was a member of parliament or there was an official in the SDS who was named was Vjestica. I believe he came from Bosanska Krupa and I think I did meet him once about a month before the war broke out in Bosanska Krupa. I mean he was easy to remember because of his rather specific last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. He apparently told the assembly that in the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa there were only 24 per cent of Serbs and 14.500 and 47.000 Muslims. He also told the assembly that: "For a year and a half, we have been preparing for war in the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa because we knew that there would be war and it cannot be avoided." You yourself were in Prijedor, which like Krupa, had a majority of Muslims. Were you aware of any preparations in Prijedor for war by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: We of course were aware of the war going on in Croatia, and secondly, we were also aware that the Yugoslav People's Army was planning to wage war in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We became aware of that when they had moved all their forces from Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina rather than choose Serbia which would have been logical. And of course, judging by the conduct of people returning from the front, the behaviour of the SDS officials, and army officers in that area, it was quite logical that war preparations were underway, or rather, it was evident. At that time, at that time, the SDS was actively and publicly taking part in preparations for war. One could hardly fail to -- one could hardly notice specific preparations by the SDS. Vjestica says here that they had been preparing for it for about a year and a half; that is before the elections. Frankly speaking, we did not notice that they were doing it on the eve of the elections, at the time of the elections or on the -- in the wake of the elections or perhaps it was very secret. But the fact is that when the war broke out, people who were experts, people who understand things about wars and fighting, that they observed that the operations were following plans and were being conducted in a manner indicative of a long-term preparation rather than a 15-day preparation for it or a month or three months.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move, then, please, to Kupresanin? Whose speech in the translation starts at page 28? In fact, think we can leave it, because he talked about the military for the most part and can we come then finally to Mr. Brdjanin? And let's have a look at that. Page 29. Now, Mr. Brdjanin said this, "Mr. President, I've asked for the floor only after I realised that I was the most remote, that compared to everyone else I was kindergarten. I would first of all like to thank those participating in the discussion. I would like to say a heart-felt bravo to Mr. Kalinic. In all my appearances in this joint assembly, it has never crossed my mind that though he seems quiet, while I seem hawkish, his opinions are the closest to mine. I believe that this is the formula and we should adhere to this formula." Now, Mr. Brdjanin expressed the same surprise that you did about Mr. Kalinic, apparently, but he stated that he seemed hawkish. Was that the impression that you got when he was making speeches in the Sarajevo assembly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: My impression, at least when he spoke about the above-mentioned topic, that he was very energetic, that sometimes his position sounded like ultimatums, that he was intolerant and he was saying, I'm not quoting him, but that the Serb people would do it, the people of Bosanska Krajina would do something regardless of the position of the parliament. And he spoke in a rather aggressive manner so that one got the impression -- I wouldn't like to use the word belligerently because I do not remember him mentioning war or saying that we would wage war, but he was very aggressive and pretty arrogant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He then dealt with, in his speech, the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, which I want to come back to, and then the question of Muslims in the JNA. He stated this, at page -- it's page 30, paragraph beginning, "How can anyone still believe it's all right that we have a Muslim teaching political classes in the Banja Luka Corps?" Had you come across anybody called Lieutenant Colonel Hasotic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as I say, the rest of the speech which was fairly lengthy, dealt with the question of the armed forces mobilisation. And then finally, at page 32, he said, "Unfortunately, as Mr. Kalinic has said, to wage war by -- because it seems to me that this is our option, our only option." Just so we can finish this before the break, page 32, Mr. Ostojic spoke, and do you know who Mr. Ostojic was, Velibor Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I do, yes. He was a prominent member of the SDS and he was a minister in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he said that he noted that he fully agreed with the view expressed by our colleague, Minister Kalinic, and later on stated that he'd witnessed a confirmation of what Mr. Brdjanin said about the Muslims and their conduct in relation to Serbian rule. Then can we look, please, at Mr. Kozic at page 33? Who was Mr. Kozic? Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I knew him, yes. He was a Serb member of parliament from Herzegovina. I'm not sure whether he was a member of the Serb Radical Party or the Serb Democratic Party. I'm not sure about that. I do remember however that he was involved in an affair which has to do with arms contraband. It became public and I believe that he was stripped of his seat in the parliament after that. I think it was Mr. Kozic, but I'm quite sure that he represented Herzegovina in the parliament. I think his first name was Dusan, that he was Dusan Kozic or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, he dealt with the enemy, as he described them, "Ustashas and mujahedin must be defeated by whatever means are necessary and only after that can we negotiate." The terms "mujahedin and Ustashas" were used by nearly every speaker. Before the walkout of the Serbs in October, 1991, were those sort of terms used within the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then finally, effectively, there was various short speeches and a very lengthy rambling speech from Mladic. How often did the military turn up in the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer this question, but I know on what occasions under when is it that the military can appear in a parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That is, they will turn up there if they are invited to do so by the state, by the government, by the parliament, to have a general there submit a -- and have him submit a report, or perhaps an officer may be there as a candidate for one of the portfolios in the government if the parliament decides so. These are the legal possibilities allowing for a general or another army officer to sit in -- to sit in the parliament, or in case of the state of war or preparation for war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the problem that we just saw was that the question that Ms. Korner asked was not properly translated and so Mr. Sejmenovic was answering what he thought the question was. And as I understand it, what she was asking him was how often the military turned up in the assembly, and that's not what he heard in translation, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that is the case, and I'm not in a position to confirm or deny that, perhaps the question can be put again and Mr. Sejmenovic can try to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It looks like an answer to me, interestingly enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What Mr. Ackerman is suggesting --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not worth pursuing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- based probably on what his assistant is -- has explained to him, is that the -- your question was not properly interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not going to pursue it, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, can we ask for a break here because I want to look at the video of the 12th of May and just identify the persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will break for 25 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've given Ms. Chuqing the transcript reverences that you've asked for. They are just handwritten on one copy. That's the best I could do for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a copy as well? I don't need it straight away, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, I think Mr. Sejmenovic you had an opportunity to look on Friday at a video. I'm going to ask you to have a look at it please again and could you say "stop" when you recognised somebody? I think that's the easiest way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we play the video V0001983? Is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so because I don't see anything on my video, on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what I mean. I'm asking the video people if there is a problem. I don't know whether the video booth heard. Could we play, please, the video marked V0001983.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, as soon as you recognise somebody could you say "stop"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. I see here General Talic, next to him is General Mladic. In the second row, I think I see Mr. Vucurevic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Carry on, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. This is Mr. Krajisnik, president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time when he was in it. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next to Krajisnik is also a member of parliament, I don't remember his name but I remember him. Again, General Talic, Mladic. Stop. Mr. Brdjanin is standing in the third row between two windows. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. I think that on the right-hand side is a Serb politician from Croatia, Goran Hadzic. It seems to me it's him. It looks like him, but I'm not quite sure. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the left-hand side, we see Mr. Koljevic, next to him is Mr. Velibor Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause there for a for a moment, please, which one is Ostojic and which one is Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The elderly gentleman on the right wearing spectacles is Professor Koljevic, member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. In the middle is Mr. Velibor Ostojic, member of the SDS and minister in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Later on, he was minister in the entity or rather state that the Serbs were building. This is Mr. Ostojic, whose speech in parliament we considered during the previous sitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again here we see Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. Here we see Mr. Kupresanin. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I remember many of the people who are on this video footage but I can't remember their names. For the most part they are former Members of Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Again, General Talic and General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all. Although I played that video in opening, it never was exhibited yet, so can we make it P1531, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is being so admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is being so admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sejmenovic, I just want to deal fairly quickly with matters that happened to you before we look at some photographs and one more video. You, I think, described what happened after the takeover in Prijedor to the Stakic Judges, and you then dealt with the meeting that was held with the SDS in Prijedor, and then the attack which took place on Kozarac on the 24th of May. And I also think you gave a lengthy -- or gave lengthy evidence both in chief and under cross-examination about the organisation of the Muslim TO in Kozarac. Now, I think that you yourself went into hiding after the attack but eventually went to Trnopolje, which by then had been turned into this camp, and from there, you were taken to Prijedor, first of all to the police station where you were beaten, and finally to Omarska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before we deal with the video in relation to Omarska or about which you've been asked on a number of occasions but so the judges can see it, can I just ask you to have a look at some photographs, please? First -- some have already been exhibited, others not. Can you look first of all, please, at one which has been marked with ERN number 01002441? Do you recognise that, Mr. Sejmenovic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I recognise it. This is the camp of Omarska on this photograph, or rather before the war, these were the facilities of the Omarska mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to remind you, these were the ones taken in 2000 by Mr. Inayat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you look, please, next?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is going to be exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There is a collection, I gather, of photographs P1128.38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then second one -- can we just give it to the witness and then we'll hand them out afterwards. We'll put it on the ELMO. Do you recognise that as an aerial view of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's it. These are the facilities of the mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just -- I'm sorry, can you just indicate where is Trnopolje in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this camp, Trnopolje is in this direction here. In the direction in which I'm pointing this pointer. So it's over here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That will be, Your Honour, .39. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you have a look, two shots of aerial, first of all, 24 -- I'm sorry, I'm told these are already exhibited. Already distributed. This is 2428. What are we looking at there, please, Mr. Sejmenovic?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The area of Kozarac and, in the background, the mountain of Kozara. The road that we see in the middle of the photograph is the Banja Luka-Prijedor road or rather the Prijedor-Banja Luka road and the road that I'm showing now is the Kozarac-Trnopolje road.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm just looking for my note of something.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you this about that photograph for a moment. Yeah. Can you indicate where the artillery was stationed during the attack on Kozarac on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: On this photograph, I can show the directions involved or some places. The artillery was on Kozara, on Benkovac. I think it's in this area here, around here approximately. It was in this area, above the quarry. It was in this area, in the direction of this road, and then below the road in the area of Vrapci [phoen]. It was above the road, but further on, in the area of Orlovci and further on in the area of Urija. It was on the opposite side towards Trnopolje and further on towards Ribnjak, and Tomasica. It was in the area of Omarska in this direction, so these are some of the localities where there was artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then finally, the photograph marked 0 -- sorry, that will be, Your Honour, that's 1128-40.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally, could you have a look at 01002426? All right. I don't think it matters much, Your Honour, because we seem to be -- you've already got it but -- thanks. Now, looking again it's another aerial shot. Can you just indicate where Trnopolje was -- is, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: This is Kozarac from the opposite direction, in relation to the other direction that we were viewing it from. So now Kozarac is here closer to me, and these are the slopes of Mount Kozara and the villages in Kozara and this is the road towards Trnopolje. Trnopolje is in this area. Behind Trnopolje are Ribnaca [phoen], Sanicani and then Tomasica. So Trnopolje is below Kozarac in this area. It can't be seen well in this photograph, but it is located in the area that I'm pointing out right now. On the right-hand side further on we see the road, Prijedor-Banja Luka, the Prijedor-Banja Luka road and what we see here, at the very end of this photograph, is probably the outskirts of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be 1128.41. Your Honour, it's not -- you can actually just make out, it's better on the original rather than on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think you were then in Omarska for sometime before you were taken out of Omarska by Kupresanin, apparently on the orders of Karadzic because you overheard a conversation between Kupresanin and Karadzic. But whilst you were there, were you interviewed by Serb Television?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask now that that be played.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's actually -- there is a lengthy -- effectively what it was was Penny Marshall being followed around by Serb television. I think I'm going to ask if they can find it -- I didn't set it out because I was going to play the whole video, but I don't think that's necessary -- the part where it says -- it's on the transcript, if Your Honours have got it, reporter -- maybe it's just quicker to play the whole thing through. Your Honour, I will just ask the video be played and then I'll stop it after the -- the number is S151, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Prijedor looks quite dismal after the fighting and villages were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the sound any longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I suggest the interpreter doesn't bother to interpret because there is a transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Pause, please. Can we stop the video, please, and go back? Can we reverse the video until I say stop, please? Stop. Stop. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic do you recognise the road with the destroyed buildings on it? Stop the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: It could be one of the several roads by which there were destroyed houses. This is the old road or the road Prijedor-Banja Luka, the old road through Kamicani. It could be the road Kozarac-Trnopolje. Along all these roads there were destroyed or burned houses, a large number of houses, because it was mostly non-Serb families, non-Serb population, that lived along these roads, so I cannot state anything with certainty. I assume that they are going where they say that this TV crew is going, namely Trnopolje-Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we continue the video, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. That's all I want to play of the video. Your Honour, I'm not sure what we are calling this, oh, yes, P1532/S151.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, you've been asked about this video on a number of occasions and gave a very long explanation in the Stakic trial around page 4795 of the transcript. Just in summary, why did you say the things that you were saying there? For example blaming Mujadic for the horrors that had taken place, as we see from the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I had to because that was what they wanted to hear. Had I told what I really thought, I suppose I would have been killed after the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, you gave -- and I'm not going to give you the explanation again, a long explanation. Now, finally, Mr. Sejmenovic, I want to ask you about -- I want to go back to Mr. Brdjanin. You've described what he was like in the parliament and we've gone through the speech that he made. He became -- and there is, as I understand it, no dispute about this -- the President of the ARK, the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff. Now, in your view, from what you know of him as a person, was he someone who could have been a mere figure head in that Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, perhaps one could get that impression. However, his subsequent activity, his high ranking amongst the Serb politicians showed that that was not really the case because he was promoted and appointed to very important offices, such as, for instance, Deputy Prime Minister or Assistant Prime Minister or a ministerial position. That is what I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You started your answer by saying, "At that time perhaps one could get that impression." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I said that at that time, it could have been the case, because I do not know. I was not aware. I didn't know what were the relations within the SDS at the time. What I do know for a fact is that at least at the local level, the Serb Democratic Party at times designated to positions people for, I presume, some formal reasons and then replaced them by some other people. I'm referring to the local level. Whether it held true of the higher echelons, I do not know. What I'm saying is that this was the first important position that Mr. Brdjanin held that I heard -- that I heard of. But after that, he did not disappear from the political stage. He moved up and up to ever more important political functions so for me, it is logical to think that he was not a figure-head but I'm saying this is my opinion and my impression.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm more interested in from what you knew of his personality and the type of speeches that he made whilst you were in the assembly with him, in your view, was he someone who would sit back and let someone else take the decisions? And be merely content to sign off on other people's decisions?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think so. Because I know that in Banja Luka, he had a lot of weight in the political hierarchy. Once Mr. Kupresanin took me to the parliament building, I overheard a fragment of conversation of some Serb politicians and they were mentioning Mr. Brdjanin and from the context, I gathered that they were -- that Brdjanin, Kupresanin, were on very poor terms, because at that time, Kupresanin referred to Mr. Brdjanin adversely. He mentioned some state reserves, petrol, fuel, but I overheard only a fragment of that conversation and I cannot really give it to you verbatim. I also know that they were part of the local political structures but that they advocated different options. Kupresanin lost his positions eventually and Brdjanin continued to move up. I was also interested in the fate of a colleague, a Serb politician, with whom I was on very good terms. He came from a place called Celinac, near Banja Luka and whose last name was Kuzmanovic because in the early days of the war I never heard his name mentioned publicly. And then the gentleman whom I asked about him told me that that Kuzmanovic had lost his influence and that he had got into some trouble because of Brdjanin because allegedly Brdjanin came from the same area. And refugees from Celinac, who arrived in September, sometime in early September, in Bosanska Vrbanja, they were saying, at least according to what they said, that their houses had been burnt and that they had been expelled because it had been done by some local officials following the orders of Mr. Brdjanin. Now, I am giving you the talk of semi-literate people, men and women, that I heard. But I know that this Kuzmanovic who was a friend of mine, he was not a prominent figure and Mr. Brdjanin made a career, made head way in politics, but that is all that I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's going to take me a few minutes to get organised. I'll do it as fast as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you require any help, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have a lot of things that I want to talk to you about, and I have no idea how long it's going to take, but let me tell you this. I'm going to try to ask you questions, as much as I'm able to, that you should be able to answer fairly easily. Some of them I think you should be able to answer with a simple yes or no. But the amount of time you spend here is going to depend to a great extent on the length of the answers that you give, and so if you will try to listen to my questions, try to understand what I'm asking you, and give the shortest possible answers and just answer the question that I'm asking you, I think we can move through this fairly quickly. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, that's the advice that we give you as well. Try to answer the question, the whole question and nothing but the question. We don't want whole stories, not exactly related to the question that is being asked or that is being put to you. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first thing I want to ask you about is whether by any chance you have been watching this trial or listening to it by any of the means that are available for you to do that? Have you seen any part of this trial?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you a member -- are you a member of any kind of an association of detainees or former camp inmates or any association of that kind?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you ever been?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Not personally, no. Whether somebody put my name on a list without my knowledge, without telling me that, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You certainly -- from your knowledge, you're not a member of any such association; correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember enrolling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm not asking you that question because I know the answer. I'm asking you because I'm trying to find out, okay?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, I've already told you. I did not, how did they put together, lists in the various associations I do not know that. Perhaps some put my name somewhere because they knew that I had been to the camp, but I never joined actively any such association.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I suggest to you, sir, and I put it to you, sir, that in your various testimonies and statements regarding the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that to some extent you've simply made up answers because you believe they sounded good in the context of the testimony you were giving. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's a wrap up question. I suggest Mr. Ackerman puts each individual thing he says he made up rather than a general statement like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, your objection is sustained, Ms. Korner. I don't suppose that you're suggesting to the witness that he made up all his testimony in the Stakic and in other cases and what he told us this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My question was clear in that regard too, Your Honour. I didn't suggest that everything was made up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I mean, if it not everything, if there is anything in particular that you're suggesting has been made up by the witness, then you should indicate that and put the direction -- the question as direct -- as direct as you would like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's -- will definitely happen, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first thing that I want to talk with you about, sir, is your statement to the OTP. And you mentioned a bit of this in your testimony this morning also. It probably would be helpful for you to have a copy of your OTP statement dated 2nd November, 2000. I think you told us in your direct testimony a while ago that you first became acquainted with Mr. Brdjanin as when he was a member of the parliament representing Banja Luka. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: In the parliament, in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. That was your first acquaintance with Mr. Brdjanin when he was there representing Banja Luka. Is that what your testimony is?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: He came to represent Banja Luka -- the area of Banja Luka in the parliament. I came from Prijedor. Everybody came from a different area. I began to notice him in the parliament, that is, he became somebody whom I saw at the parliamentary sessions. Before that, I did not know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Don't you know that Mr. Brdjanin never was a member of parliament from Banja Luka? Don't you know that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin was a member of parliament from the area of Banja Luka, sir. The area of Banja Luka is pretty large. I did not mean -- I did not mean the municipality or the town of Banja Luka, but the region of Banja Luka, the region whose capital, whose principal city is Banja Luka. I cannot remember exactly, but I think that Mr. Brdjanin was on the -- was a member of the Chamber of Citizens. I'm not quite sure but I think so, and MPs, the Chamber of Citizens, were elected from larger constituencies and that was called the constituency of Banja Luka so I think there is a misunderstanding here. I think you understood -- you didn't understand it in the way that I interpreted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you represented the municipality of Prijedor, and in that representation, you were able, for instance, to attend and did attend meetings of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: At times, when I was in Prijedor, if I didn't have a session to attend in Sarajevo at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want you to refer to -- I'm going to refer to your statement to the Prosecutor now. It says page 2 at the bottom but it's actually the first page of your statement in the English version. You talk about what Mr. Brdjanin said and you give an example. For example, in the autumn of 1992, Brdjanin said on television that non-Serbs did not need wood for the winter. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier on, I -- that is before the break, I gave you this example. This is what I heard from rank and file, non-Serb people, who were not active, who were just ordinary people, who listened to the radio hour after hour because they lived in fear and they didn't know what was in store for them, and I think I said that on several occasions during this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: As I said when we started, you're going to be here a very long, long time if you don't answer my questions. The question was simple. In your statement, you said, in the autumn of 1992, Brdjanin said on television that non-Serbs did not need wood for the winter. Isn't that the case? Isn't that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I did not say who I heard it from and whether I watched it. It does not here I saw on television because that is not what it says here. Had I seen it on television, I would have told Their Honours I saw it on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where were you in the autumn of 1992, when this statement, you think, was made on television?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know when it was, when the statement was made on television and when I heard it from people who said had heard it. It was the autumn of 1992, in Bosanska Vrbanja, which is a Banja Luka suburb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
